title: How coaches say lead, and how to translate it
summary: Coaches describe lead in feet, target widths, barrel widths and clock positions. How to understand each one and pass it on without changing the coach’s picture.

body.html: Units first. British and American coaches talk about lead in feet and yards: “give it four foot” (British for four feet), “two feet in front”. Coaches from continental Europe often use metres. One foot is about 30 cm and one yard about 0.9 m. But a lead number is not a measurement. It describes the gap the coach wants the shooter to see between the muzzles and the target at the moment of the shot: his “picture”. So keep his number and unit. Do not convert it in the middle of an instruction. If the shooter asks, explain roughly between targets.
Take the shot yourself: the result gives the lead in metres, feet and target widths, and how small that gap looks at the muzzle.
body.heading: Watch how the lead works

body.html: The gap the shooter sees at the muzzle, the perceived lead, is much smaller than the real distance in the air. That is one more reason to keep the coach’s words instead of turning them into metres.

Target widths: “half a bird”, “a bird’s width”, “a clay’s length”. Here “bird” means the target, not a real bird. Barrel widths: “a barrel’s width” or “two barrels” mean the gap the shooter sees at the muzzle. Careful: “two barrels” can also be about the gun. If both barrels went off together (the gun “doubled”), it is a double discharge. “Two barrels” can also mean that the target was shot with both barrels. If it is not clearly about lead, ask.

Relative words: “more”, “less”, “a touch more”, “double it”, “half that”, “same lead”. Keep them relative and do not invent a number. “Same lead” matters a lot: it tells the shooter not to add lead after a miss.

Directions: “in front” and “behind” refer to the way the target is flying. “Over” means the same as “high”, and “under” the same as “low”. Coaches use a clock face in two ways. Laid over the target, 12 o’clock is the top and 3 o’clock the right side, as the shooter sees it: “you hit it at six” means the bottom edge. Laid over the field, 12 is straight ahead: “it comes from eleven” means slightly left.
Left and right on the target become “in front” or “behind” only once you know which way it flies. On a target going right to left, a shot cloud (the pattern) at two o’clock is high and behind it.

Method: pass on the number, the unit, what it is compared with (a bird, a barrel) and the direction, exactly and briefly, in the coach’s rhythm. If something is unclear, ask him one word: “Feet?” All of this is for training: in competition coaching is forbidden.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Give the lead the coach calls “four feet”; it describes his picture, so keep his number and unit.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Add half a target’s width to the lead picture.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Make the lead picture twice as big as last time.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Same lead, just keep it moving.
phrases.meaning: The lead was right; the miss came from stopping the gun.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: That one goes right to left. You were at two o’clock: a touch lower and more in front.
phrases.meaning: On a target flying right to left, the shot cloud (the pattern) went above and behind it, at two o’clock on the target. Shoot slightly lower and give a little more lead.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Keep a gap the width of the barrel, as seen at the muzzle, ahead of the target.

key_points.html: Keep the coach’s number and unit; do not convert lead mid-instruction.
Bird = target: “half a bird” is half a target’s width.
Relative words stay relative; “same lead” must be translated.
Clock on the target: 12 is the top; clock on the field: 12 is straight ahead.
“Two barrels” is not always a lead: it may be a double discharge or a target shot with both barrels — ask.

quiz.q: The coach says “Give it four foot” to a shooter who thinks in metres. What do you say?
quiz.explain: A lead number is the coach’s picture. Converting it mid-instruction adds false precision or errors, and “four metres” changes the meaning completely. If the shooter asks, explain roughly between targets.

options.text: Half the width of a target
A target that broke in two
A small bird near the trap

quiz.explain: In clay shooting “bird” means the target, so the coach asks for half a target’s width of lead.

quiz.q: The coach says “Same lead, keep it moving”. Why must “same lead” be translated?

options.text: It is a call the referee uses
Otherwise the shooter may add lead and miss
It is a polite greeting between shooters
It changes the order of the targets

quiz.explain: After a miss many shooters add lead by themselves. “Same lead” tells them the cause was the stopped gun, not the lead.
